title: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
shortTitle: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
summary: This sub-technique is lateral movement performed by importing a stolen Kerberos ticket rather than typing a password. Tickets are the domain's normal proof of identity: a ticket granting ticket is presented to the key distribution centre to obtain service tickets, and a service ticket is presented directly to one resource. An attacker who extracts either from the memory of a logged-on session, or who forges one with key material, can inject it into their own session and reach whatever the ticket authorises. Where the ticket was forged rather than stolen, no corresponding authentication event appears in the key distribution centre log, which is the classic mismatch that detection targets. Useful evidence includes the Kerberos service ticket request events, the encryption type and ticket options requested, the source host of the presentation, and the account's normal working systems. Comparing those against baseline is what separates genuine reuse from everyday single sign-on behaviour.

beginner.definition: In a Windows network, a ticket is a small digital pass that proves you already signed in. It lets you reach servers without typing your password again. This sub-technique is when an attacker steals a ticket and shows it to servers to act as you.
beginner.whyItMatters: A ticket can open one specific server, or it can be used to ask for many more tickets. Attackers move through a network without any password and often without any visible login prompt. Servers accept the ticket because it is real, so nothing looks broken.
howItWorks: When you sign in to a Windows network, the domain hands you a ticket.
You show that ticket to get smaller tickets for each server you need.
The tickets sit in the memory of your logged-on session while you work.
An attacker with administrator rights on that machine copies a ticket from memory.
They add it to their own session, then show it to the server that accepts it.
Because the pass is genuine, the server grants access as if you had signed in yourself.
beginner.example: Picture a theatre with a cloakroom. You show your coat check ticket and the attendant hands over the coat, no questions asked. A thief who picks up your ticket from the floor can collect your coat. The attendant never sees the theft. The ticket looks perfect because it is perfect. Only the person holding it has changed.
takeaways: Tickets are reusable passes, so any compromise of a session risks them.
A ticket used without a matching login record is a strong warning sign.
Limit where domain administrators sign in to reduce the tickets available to steal.

objectives: Explain the roles of the ticket granting ticket and the service ticket.
Describe how a ticket is taken from one session and used in another.
Explain why a forged ticket leaves no matching request in the domain log.
Identify the Kerberos events and fields used to spot unusual ticket use.
Explain why the source host of a ticket presentation matters for detection.
